description:
Phobos and Deimos have orbited Mars side by side for billions of years, quietly watching the Red Planet. Now they’ve come down to Earth on a new mission: finding places that could help humans prepare for life on Mars. Lucky for them, they landed in Egypt, home to some of the most Mars-like deserts on Earth! 

We’re two computer engineering students at the German University in Cairo (GUC), using NASA data to find Earth analogs for future Moon bases and Mars sites, starting with our own backyard.
summary:
Twin Sands will take you, with all your senses, on a journey to Mars, the Moon, and the places on Earth that secretly look just like them, with a little hanging rover as your guide the whole way. You'll walk through red dust, hear the real winds recorded by NASA's Perseverance rover, smell the rust and the burnt powder of the Moon, and feel what the ground is like under your boots.

On the way, you discover that pieces of Mars and the Moon are already hiding on Earth: deserts, craters and icy lands that are their twins.

Watch Earth's land squeeze into a ball the size of Mars. Follow trails of air, soil and water across all three worlds. Walk real 3D terrain of Gale Crater, Jezero and Olympus Mons with a talking rover, or the Moon's south pole and highlands with an astronaut by your side.

Then meet each twin. We compared every Moon and Mars site with Earth locations around the world using real data from NASA, ESA, CSA and JAXA: terrain, temperature, ground heat and minerals. Each pair gets a Twin Score that shows how alike they are, which helps choose where to train astronauts and test rovers.

And we went out ourselves, to find Mars right here in Egypt's deserts and shared our trips!
details:
From a squeezing Earth to a dust storm on Mars to a footprint on the Moon, Twin Sands is a five-stop journey, with a little hanging rover as your guide!

The five stops:

  • Meet Mars: watch all of Earth's land squeeze into a ball almost exactly the size of Mars, then meet its two tiny moons circling around it.
  • Twin Trails: Rust, Soil, Water, Dust and the Moon's South Pole. For each one, you first SEE a story about Mars and the Moon, told in our own voices. Then you HEAR real sounds (Perseverance's microphone on Mars, silence on the airless Moon), SMELL what each world would smell like, and FEEL how hot, cold or dry it is. Each trail ends with Earth, Mars and the Moon side by side on matching maps with one colour scale, so anyone can compare them at a glance.
  • Explore: walk real 3D terrain built from elevation data, at Gale Crater, Jezero Crater (inside a khamaseen dust storm) and Olympus Mons (with a then-and-now eruption slider) on Mars, and at Shackleton, Malapert and the lunar highlands on the Moon. A talking rover on Mars, or an astronaut leaving bootprints on the Moon, walks with you and explains what you're seeing. Each walk has a field task: follow a beam of light to find real NASA hardware (Ingenuity, Viking, the Apollo 16 lander, a habitat, a radio dish, a greenhouse), then fly, launch or switch it on
  • Twin Score: pick a Moon or Mars site and meet its closest Earth twin, with real photos, height maps, a side-view profile, and every number behind the match.
  • Boots on the Ground: our own trips to the deserts of Egypt and Saudi Arabia, where Mars is right here on Earth.

HOW IT WORKS

1- Twin Trails: real maps, real sounds

Each trail is built from real data, shown on the same colour scale for all three worlds so they can be compared directly:

  • Rust: iron-rich ground on Mars and the Moon (NASA Mars Trek and Moon Trek, Clementine iron map) next to Earth's red deserts.
  • Soil: how much the ground heats and cools between day and night. Earth uses JAXA GCOM-C land temperature (day and night), Mars uses TES thermal inertia (NASA PDS), the Moon uses LRO Diviner.
  • Water: where water hides. Mars Odyssey's water map (NASA PDS), Lunar Prospector hydrogen on the Moon, and ESA CCI permafrost on Earth, plus a CSA RADARSAT-1 radar image of Haughton Crater taken in the dark of polar night.
  • Dust: Earth's dust from NASA MERRA-2 (via GIBS) next to the Mars dust cover map.
  • South Pole: LRO maps of the Moon's south pole, where sunlight and shadow decide where a base can go.

The sounds are real recordings: Perseverance's microphone on Mars, and field recordings on Earth. The Moon stays silent on purpose, because there is no air to carry sound.

2- Explore: walking on real ground

The three Mars walks (Gale, Jezero, Olympus Mons) and the three Moon walks (Shackleton, Malapert, the highlands) are built from real elevation models: MRO CTX and MOLA/HRSC on Mars, LRO LOLA on the Moon. The ground under your feet is the real shape of the place, and a 120 km backdrop of real terrain fills the horizon. The rover is NASA's Perseverance 3D model and speaks with the browser's voice. Each walk has its own weather and ground: layered rocks at Gale, a khamaseen dust storm at Jezero (the rover wears storm gear), and lava fields with a then-and-now eruption slider at Olympus Mons. On the Moon, the astronaut leaves bootprints and talks over radio "beeps", like Apollo.

3- Twin Score: finding the twins

For each site we read a 12 km window of real measurements: height and roughness (Copernicus DEM on Earth, CTX on Mars, LOLA on the Moon), slope, surface temperature and its day-to-night swing, thermal inertia (how fast the ground heats and cools), brightness and minerals. Each feature becomes a percentile so three different worlds can be compared fairly, and the Twin Score is the average closeness across seven features. It is a transparent ranking, not a black box: the site shows which features match and which don't, and never pretends a match where data is missing. We checked our ranking against real NASA analog test sites such as Haughton Crater, the Atacama Desert and Mauna Kea.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Astronauts and rovers are trained and tested on Earth before they fly, and choosing the right analog site saves money, time and risk. Twin Sands makes that choice open, repeatable and easy to understand.

It is also for everyone. Anyone, with no science background, can learn what Mars and the Moon are really like and how much they have in common with our own planet: the same red dust, the same cold deserts, the same frozen ground. Seeing a piece of Mars in a desert you can drive to truly opens people's minds. Space stops feeling far away, and becomes something you can understand, feel and even visit. That matters most in places like Egypt and Saudi Arabia, where Mars-like land is right next door, and where we hope the next generation of space explorers will start their journey.

You can also find the Mars nearest you, or swipe between a Mars place and its Earth twin.

TOOLS

  • Website: React, TypeScript, Vite, three.js with React Three Fiber (3D terrain and models), Framer Motion (animation), Web Audio API (live sound design), Web Speech API (rover voice).
  • Data pipeline: Python with rasterio, NumPy and Pillow, reading data from NASA, ESA, CSA, JAXA and USGS.

WHY IT'S CREATIVE

Most data sites ask you to read charts. Twin Sands asks you to travel. We used very little text and a lot of visuals, sound and movement, so the data is something you experience, not just read. Every planet has its own voice, sounds, ground and weather, and every comparison is backed by real measurements.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

  • Honesty: a twin that matches in temperature but not in height is labelled that way; the site does not pick safe landing or habitat sites.
  • Fair comparison: the same 12 km window and the same scales for all three worlds.
  • Accessibility: simple words, big visuals, and it works in any modern browser with no install.
  • Using as many challenge resources as possible: 10 of the 11 listed, including NASA PDS, LRO, Earthdata, GIBS, CSA RADARSAT-1, ESA Copernicus and Open Science Catalog, and JAXA G-Portal.

DATA SOURCES

Real data from four space agencies powers every part of Twin Sands.

NASA → the heart of the project. Through NASA's Planetary Data System, we used LRO Diviner temperatures for every Moon site, TES thermal inertia for Mars, and Mars Odyssey's water map, which shows where water hides under the Martian ground. LRO's LOLA heights and LROC photos let us rebuild the Moon's south pole and highlands as real 3D ground you can walk on, and MRO's CTX elevation models did the same for Gale, Jezero and Olympus Mons. NASA Earthdata Search gave us EMIT minerals, ECOSTRESS temperatures and MODIS brightness for every Earth location we compared, and NASA Worldview (GIBS) gave us Earth maps of dust, snow and land temperature for the Twin Trails. Real sounds from Perseverance's microphone, NASA photos, and NASA's Perseverance 3D model bring it all to life.

ESA → Copernicus DEM gave us the height of every Earth location in the Twin Score, and Sentinel-2 images show what each Earth twin looks like from above. Through ESA's Open Science Catalog, we found the CCI permafrost map, which shows Earth's frozen ground next to Mars' in the Water trail.

CSA → a RADARSAT-1 radar image of Haughton Crater in Canada, taken in the dark of polar night in January 2001, read and displayed by following CSA's SAR Python tutorial. It shows how radar sees through darkness, just like it would at the Moon's shadowed south pole.

JAXA → GCOM-C land temperature data, from JAXA G-Portal, gave us Earth's day-to-night temperature swing, compared in the Soil trail with how fast the ground heats and cools on Mars and the Moon.
